1:
Six years of Athaliah's usurpation lie behind the chapter's opening, and the witnesses read its first verse as the moment the long night breaks. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the scene: after the boy Joash had been kept in hiding for six years, the high priest Jehoiada came to the resolution to make an end of the tyranny of Athaliah and to raise the young prince to the throne, a plan carried out here and completed in the next chapter. They note at once that the Chronicler tells the story alongside the fuller record of 2 Kings 11:4-20, where the events are in several points more briefly narrated and, on the surface, differently represented — in Kings the high priest seems chiefly to have leaned on the royal body-guard, while here the Levites come to the fore.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the bare notice into a hymn of restored providence. We may well imagine the bad posture of affairs in Jerusalem during Athaliah's six years, he says, and wonder that God permitted it and his people bore it so long; but after such a dark and tedious night the returning day was the brighter and the more welcome. The continuance of David's seed and throne was what God had sworn by his holiness in Ps. 89:35, and an interruption was no defeasance; the stream of government here runs again in its right channel. Henry draws Jehoiada in five strokes — a man of great prudence, who reserved the prince until the nation had wearied of the usurper; of great interest, whom captains and Levites obeyed at a word; of great faith, moved not by his wife's kinship to the royal house but by regard to the word of God; of great religion, guarding the temple from profanation; and of great resolution, who ventured his own head in a good cause and went through with it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the Chronicler's very verbs. "Jehoiada strengthened himself" means he showed himself strong and behaved boldly, the courage urged in 1 Samuel 4:9; it is the writer's favourite word, substituted for the plainer "Jehoiada sent" of Kings. The names of the five captains of hundreds are added here and not found in the parallel, introduced, Ellicott observes, in the Chronicler's well-known manner, his style very visible in every such addition — compare the doubled Azariah of 2 Chron. 21:2. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke simply lays out the chapter's course — Jehoiada proclaims and anoints Joash, Athaliah is slain, the people covenant to serve the Lord, Baal's temple is thrown down — and refers the reader to the same events at 2 Kings 11:4. The voices do not divide; together they open the chapter as the recovery of a throne God had bound himself to keep.
2:
The revolution begins not with soldiers but with a summons, and the witnesses mark how the Chronicler widens the circle of those who share in it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that this verse and the next are the Chronicler's own contribution to the story: where the book of Kings moves straight to Jehoiada's charge to the captains of the guard, here the priest's agents first go about in Judah — the same circuit of the land that teaching Levites had made in 2 Chron. 17:9, and Samuel on his yearly rounds in 1 Samuel 7:16 — to gather the Levites out of all the cities and the chief of the fathers, the heads of the clans, up to Jerusalem. The parallel account is nearly, if not altogether, silent about the Levites' part in the Restoration; and Ellicott takes the Chronicler to have supplemented that account from other authorities, perhaps from Levitical traditions, precisely as his general practice and the special purpose of his history would lead one to expect.

Ellicott is at pains, however, to defend the Chronicler's fidelity. Allowing for his characteristic additions, interpretations, and substitutions of phrase for phrase, the narrative absolutely coincides with that of Kings — treating the same events, rigidly observing the same limits, maintaining a general identity of language — so that we must conclude he worked from a historical text containing sections substantially identical with the present books of Kings, yet carrying many details those books did not keep. The added matter, in other words, is not invention but a fuller record.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the gathering as the first stage of a plan laid with great care, in which all the congregation, once assembled, made a covenant with the king in the house of God, and Jehoiada then set out the day's arrangements division by division. What both witnesses see in the verse is the breadth of the thing. The throne is not restored by a knot of conspirators in a palace but by the covenant people acting through their proper representatives — the Levites who serve the sanctuary and the heads of the fathers' houses who lead the clans, summoned out of every city in Judah. The restoration of David's heir is made a national and covenantal act, gathered up into the house of God itself, so that when the boy is at last brought out and crowned it is the whole ordered community of Israel, and not a faction, that receives him. The Chronicler's fuller telling, Ellicott insists, does not swell the facts; it only lets the people of God, and not the palace guard alone, stand where they belonged in the day of the king's return.
3:
The covenant sworn in the house of God is where the witnesses locate the theological ground of the whole enterprise. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott identifies the parties to it: all the congregation — the assembled Levites and family chiefs together with the royal guard — bound themselves with the young king. He compares the phrasing with 2 Kings 11:4, where Jehoiada "made a covenant for them," that is, imposed a compact upon them and made them swear fidelity to the prince, much as a covenant was struck with a new ruler in 2 Samuel 5:3. He renders the priest's declaration less as a bare prediction than as an acclamation — "Behold the king's son! Let him be king" — and presses the closing clause: "as the LORD hath said" points back to the oracle delivered through Nathan concerning the sons of David in 2 Samuel 7:4-17. The coronation, on Ellicott's reading, is the keeping of a promise older than the crisis it resolves.

That is precisely the note the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had already sounded in his portrait of Jehoiada. What moved the high priest, he insists, was not common equity, and still less his wife's kinship to the royal family, but a regard to the word of God and the divine entail of the crown: "The king's son shall reign, must reign, as the Lord hath said." His eye to the promise, and his dependence upon it, added a great deal of glory to the undertaking. The little word "must" carries Henry's whole point — the throne of David could be usurped for six years but not abolished, because a divine entail lay upon it.

Set against the chapter's backdrop the confession is bold. Athaliah had done her worst to extinguish the royal seed, and to human eyes the line of David had all but failed; yet here stands a king's son, hidden and preserved, and the priest grounds his right not on the swords gathered around him but on what the LORD had said. The two witnesses converge on a single conviction: the restoration is lawful because it is the fulfilment of God's own word, and the men who covenant with the boy in the sanctuary are not so much making a king as receiving the one God had already given. The oath they swear only ratifies below what heaven had settled long before through Nathan's oracle to the house of David — that a son of that house should never lack a lamp before the LORD, and that the crown belonged, of divine right, to the child now standing among them.
4:
Jehoiada's battle-order is the point at which the Chronicler's distinctive interest becomes plainest, and the witnesses read it accordingly. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that where Kings simply charges the captains of the guard, "This is the thing that ye shall do," the Chronicler adds the explanatory words that the third who enter on the sabbath belong "to the priests and to the Levites," and are to be porters of the doors — warders of the thresholds of the temple, the office defined in 1 Chron. 9:19. He grants the difficulty candidly: this can hardly be harmonized with the guardsmen of the older account, and the Chronicler may have understood the words, which there designate the royal body-guard, of the sacred orders instead, thinking it impossible that any but priests and Levites should be summoned into the temple by the high priest.

Yet Ellicott refuses to let a harmonizing difficulty become a charge of dishonesty. The Chronicler may equally have had before him an account in which the part played by the priesthood was made much more of than in Kings; and in any case the priests and Levites would naturally take a large share in a movement aimed at overthrowing a rival cultus — a movement that sprang from their own spiritual head and was transacted in the very sanctuary to which they were attached. He cannot fairly be accused of arbitrary alteration, Ellicott argues, unless one first assumes that his sole source was the book of Kings, an assumption he thinks unwarranted. He recalls that the priests and Levites did duty in the temple from sabbath to sabbath, one course relieving another at the week's end, the arrangement of 1 Chron. 24, so that the sabbath changeover gave Jehoiada his natural cover.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch work at the same knot from the side of the guard, following Bertheau's reconstruction: the one company that mounted guard on the sabbath was to divide into three bands — one to keep the royal house, one to stand at the side-gate called Sur, and a third at the gate behind the runners — while the two companies going off duty were retained to watch the temple around the king. The details are intricate and the two accounts hard to lock together, but the witnesses agree on the sense: Jehoiada so disposed his men, third by third, that every approach was covered and the boy-king ringed with armed guardians at the moment of his showing. What Ellicott draws out of the tangle is a matter of proportion — that the Chronicler, writing for a community whose life centred on the restored temple, tells the same event with the Levites in the foreground where Kings had kept the guard, without falsifying a single fact of the day.
5:
The disposition of the guard continues, and the witnesses divide their attention between a gate and a principle. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the topography: the "gate of the foundation" answers to the gate called Sur in 2 Kings 11:6, which there appears as a gate of the palace, variously rendered the middle gate by the Greek and the Butchers' gate by the Syriac and Arabic. But his sharper interest is in the clause that "all the people shall be in the courts of the house of the LORD." This, he says, is written from the standpoint of a strict legalist, for whom none might enter the holy house itself save the priests; it reads almost like a protest against the older notice in 2 Kings 11:4 that Jehoiada brought the centurions of the guard into the house of the LORD. The Chronicler will have the armed laymen kept to the courts and the sanctuary reserved for those whose office admits them.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the run of verses together and identify the several bands: the Levites who are to compass the king round about, each with his weapon in his hand, are the very bodies of guards just stationed third by third, so that the later warning, "whosoever else cometh into the house shall be put to death," says in the Chronicler's idiom just what Kings meant by "whosoever cometh within the ranks" in 2 Kings 11:8. The house is to be a fortress with a sacred perimeter, and the perimeter is drawn by holiness as much as by spears.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds the small topographical gloss that ties the scene to the ground. The "gate of the foundation," he explains, was the east gate, so named because it stood lower than the other doors, at the foot of the steps by which men went up from the king's house to the temple — a detail that lets the reader picture the ascent from palace to sanctuary along which the guard was posted. Together the witnesses give the verse its double character. It is at once a piece of exact military staging — every third of the force assigned its post, the whole congregation held in the outer courts — and an assertion of the temple's inviolable holiness, so that even in an armed coup on behalf of God's anointed the line between court and sanctuary is not to be crossed. The reformation of the throne is conducted, from its first hour, under the discipline of the law of the house.
6:
The command that none but the consecrated should enter the house draws the witnesses to the theme of holiness in the midst of an armed enterprise. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes first that this verse has no counterpart in Kings; it is, he judges, an emphatic repetition of the previous direction that the people keep to the courts and not break the law by presuming into the holy chambers. Where 2 Kings 11:7 speaks of the two companies keeping "the watch of the house of the LORD," the Chronicler's closing clause, "all the people shall keep the watch of the LORD," turns the phrase to a different sense — let the people carefully observe the legal rule against entering the sanctuary. The "watch" they keep is a watch of reverence, a guarding of the boundary of the sacred.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the same words as continuous with the stationing of the guard: the priests and ministering Levites go in because they are holy, while the armed people stand without; the distinction is not one of trust but of consecration. The verse thus grounds the whole arrangement in a single principle — that access to God's house is governed by holiness and not by rank or usefulness in the day's work.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes exactly this point and makes it the crown of his praise of Jehoiada. Here was a man of great religion, he says: the matter had to be transacted in the temple, and the necessity of the case might have been thought to excuse some breach of rule; but Jehoiada gave special order that none of the people should come into the house of the LORD, but the priests and Levites only, who were holy, upon pain of death. And Henry draws the abiding lesson in a line: "Never let sacred things be profaned, no, not for the support of civil rights." The restoring of the rightful king was a just and even a holy cause, yet not so holy that it might trespass on the holiness of God's house; the end, however good, would not sanctify an irreverent means. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that in this verse the Chronicler, and Jehoiada before him, subordinate even the urgent business of the coronation to the reverence due the sanctuary — so that the reader learns, before ever the crown is set on the child's head, that the God whose promise secures the throne is a God whose house is not to be made common ground. The zeal that pulls down Baal later in this same chapter is the zeal that here fences the temple; both are the jealousy of holiness.
7:
The ring of armed men closing about the king brings to a head the one real controversy the chapter has raised, and the witnesses meet it directly. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that where Kings has Jehoiada tell the centurions, "ye shall compass the king," the Chronicler writes "the Levites shall compass the king round about, every man with his weapons in his hand." On this the critic Thenius had fastened, alleging that the Chronicler metamorphosed the guardsmen of the older account into Levites in order to divert to the priesthood the honour that properly belonged to the Praetorians. Ellicott calls the charge utterly unfair. The Chronicler dwells on the Levites' share, he grants, but he does not expressly exclude the royal guard; and the likeliest truth is that Jehoiada brought about a combination of the royal guard with the Levitical warders of the temple, the united body acting under the command of the five captains named at the outset.

The dispute, then, is genuine but one-sided among the witnesses. Thenius (as reported by Ellicott) reads the Levites as a pious fiction that robs the soldiers of their due; Ellicott, and with him the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, read them as real participants, the guards and the temple-warders fused into a single cordon. Keil indeed simply equates them: the Levites who compass the king are the bodies of guards already stationed, and the sentence "whosoever else cometh into the house shall be put to death" repeats in the Chronicler's manner the "whosoever cometh within the ranks" of 2 Kings 11:8. Ellicott adds the philological support, that "into the house" stands where Kings has the rare word for "ranks," a term that occurs only a handful of times in Scripture.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, uninterested in the source-question, presses the same reverence he found in the preceding verse: Jehoiada charged that whosoever forced his way into the house should die, so jealous was he that the sacred place not be profaned even in the tumult of the day, and that the king be kept safe within a wall of consecrated men. What the witnesses share is a refusal to pit the Levites against the guard. The armed circle around the boy is composed both of soldiers and of temple servants, and the Chronicler's stress on the latter reflects not a falsifying zeal for the priesthood but the plain fact that this was a reformation wrought in the sanctuary, by men whose own worship Athaliah's Baal had displaced. The honour was shared; the Chronicler only records the half that Kings had passed over.
8:
The execution of the plan is told with a note of wonder at its secrecy, and the witnesses gather round both the logistics and the discipline. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch observe that where Kings names "the captains of the hundreds," the Chronicler very fittingly writes "the Levites and all Judah" — that is, Judah in its chiefs — since Jehoiada had already secured the support of the heads of the fathers' houses. To the statement that even those going off duty took part, the Chronicler adds the reason: "for Jehoiada had not dismissed the courses." These courses are the divisions that, by David's arrangement in 1 Chron. 24-26, had charge of the temple service; the priest retained the outgoing week's men alongside the incoming, doubling his force at the critical hour.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms and sharpens the point. The companies whose weekly duty was fulfilled, and who would normally have been formally dismissed by the high priest, were on this emergency detained as auxiliaries to their brethren who were coming in; where Kings had merely said "they came to Jehoiada the priest," the Chronicler explains the swelling of the ranks. Both witnesses see a shrewd stroke of management in it — the sabbath changeover, which brought a double complement of Levites lawfully into the temple, was turned into the muster of a guard without arousing suspicion.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the verse from tactics to admiration. "The Levites and all Judah did as Jehoiada commanded," he notes, "and, which is strange, all that were entrusted with the secret kept their own counsel till it was executed." In a design that touched so many, over so long a preparation, not one betrayed it; and Henry finds the proverb fulfilled that "the words of the wise are heard in quiet," citing Eccl. 9:17. That whole-hearted, silent obedience is for him a mark of the cause's rightness and of Jehoiada's command over men — the same command he had traced in the priest's prudence and interest. The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the point where the plan long laid becomes deed: the Levites obey to a man, the courses are held back to strengthen the guard, and the secret kept by so many is the visible token that God, who had work to do, had qualified and animated the men to do it. What might have been a reckless conspiracy is carried through with the order of a temple service and the silence of the grave, until the moment appointed for the king's showing.
9:
The arming of the guard from the temple's own store gives the witnesses a detail rich in overtones, for the weapons put into the captains' hands had once been David's. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the verse is essentially identical with 2 Kings 11:10, save that the Chronicler names Jehoiada expressly, adds the bucklers to the spear and shields, and turns the single "spear" of the older text into "spears" — rightly, most critics judge. Each of the three words carries the article in the Hebrew, marking these as the well-known arms that had belonged to king David and were laid up in the house of God, treasures of the sort listed among his dedicated spoils in 1 Chron. 18:7.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke passes over the philology and simply refers the reader to the parallel notice of the spears and bucklers at 2 Kings 11:10, content that the two accounts describe the one act. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, reading forward into the coronation, remark that Jehoiada gave the captains the spears and shields David had presented to the temple as offerings, precisely because they had come into the temple and the arms lay ready to hand; the priest armed his men not from an arsenal but from the sanctuary's dedicated store.

There is a quiet fitness in the fact that the witnesses let stand. The child about to be crowned is David's heir, the last spark of a line Athaliah had tried to quench; and the hands that guard him are armed with David's own weapons, kept these many years in the house of the LORD. What had been dedicated to God is now taken up in the defence of God's promise to David, so that the founder of the dynasty seems, across the centuries, to arm the protectors of his threatened seed. The Chronicler's small additions — Jehoiada's name, the bucklers, the plural "spears" — all serve to fill out the picture of the high priest as the ordered, deliberate agent of the restoration, distributing consecrated arms to a consecrated guard. Keil and Ellicott agree that nothing here is improvised: the weapons, like the men, are drawn from the temple, and the whole coronation is staged within the sacred precinct and out of its holy furniture, as though the house of God were itself rising to defend the throne that God had sworn to keep. The next verses will bring the boy out into the ring of these Davidic spears to receive the crown.
10:
The armed body takes its position, and the witnesses read the verse as the drawing of a human rampart about the king. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is careful about who "the people" are here. They answer to the runners, or couriers, who "stood" in the parallel at 2 Kings 11:11, and by them the Chronicler plainly means not the mass of the congregation, held back in the outer courts, but the armed men appointed to compass the king round about, every man with his weapon in his hand, as the earlier charge of v.7 had required. The word rendered "weapon," he adds, may mean rather his missiles or arms, the same broad term used of the munitions of war in 2 Chron. 32:5, where Kings had used a commoner word; and the clause set "along by the altar and the temple" he renders as a posting of the guard toward the altar. The picture is exact: a line of armed men reaching from the right side of the house to the left, curving past the altar, with the boy-king at its centre.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, expounding the same scene, take these ranged men to be the very Levite-guards already stationed third by third, now closed into a single protecting ring for the moment of the king's appearing. Between them the two witnesses let the verse do its narrative work: everything is now in place. The congregation fills the courts; the sanctuary is fenced to the priests; and immediately about the child stands a wall of steel, weapon in every hand, stretched across the whole breadth of the temple front and bent inward by the altar.

Brief as the notice is, the witnesses feel its dramatic weight. For six years the true king had been a secret kept in an inner chamber, a life that a single betrayal would have ended; now he is set in the open, at the heart of the house of God, and the only thing between him and the usurping queen is this hedge of armed and consecrated men. The altar stands at his side, the guard at his back and flanks, and the promise of God over all. Ellicott's insistence that "the people" here are the soldiers and not the crowd guards the sense against confusion: it is not the multitude that protects the heir but the appointed few, disposed with military precision. The Chronicler has brought his reader to the very threshold of the coronation, with the stage set, the guard ranged, and the boy ringed about, so that the next verse may at last bring out the crown.
11:
The coronation itself is compressed into a handful of solemn acts, and the witnesses linger over each. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott parses the ceremony: they brought out the king's son and "put upon him the crown" — the nezer or diadem of Exod. 29:6 — "and gave him the testimony," the eduth or law, the term used of the tables laid up in the ark in Exod. 25:21. What exactly the testimony was he leaves an open question: a scroll of the ten words wrapped about the diadem, or laid upon the king's shoulder, or, as the Vulgate seems to take it, a copy of the law solemnly put into the newly crowned king's hand for him to hold — the charter of a rule bound to the word of God. He notes too that the Chronicler names "Jehoiada and his sons" as those who anointed the boy, added, as elsewhere, to make plain that it was the priests who performed the anointing, as Zadok had anointed Solomon in 1 Kings 1:39.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the shift of subject from the older account: where Kings makes Jehoiada alone the actor, the Chronicler has those present bring out and enthrone the king, while expressly naming Jehoiada and his sons — the high priest with his assisting priests — as the ones who anointed and proclaimed him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke glosses the acclamation "God save the king" as simply "May the king live!", again pointing to the parallel in 2 Kings 11:12.

It is the phrase "his sons" that draws the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley, and with him the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, into the verse's shadow. Among the sons who took a willing part in anointing Joash, Wesley observes, was Zechariah, whom this same king would afterwards ungratefully slay — the murder recorded at 2 Chron. 24:20-21. Henry sharpens the irony: it made the later crime the blacker that Zechariah had helped to set the crown on the head of the man who would one day have him stoned in the temple court. So the witnesses hold together the verse's glory and its buried grief. Here is everything a coronation should be — the crown, the law, the anointing oil, the shout of the people, the child of David lifted at last into his own — and here, unseen, stands the boy-priest whose blood the crowned child will one day shed. The testimony given into Joash's hand was meant to bind him to the LORD; the sequel will show how a king who begins under the law of God may yet turn to murder the sons of the man who made him king.
12:
The sound of the coronation reaches the palace, and the witnesses follow the usurping queen to her ruin. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the two moods side by side. First the people pleased: when the young king stood at his pillar, all the people of the land rejoiced to see, as it were, a rod sprung out of the stem of Jesse — the image of Isa. 11:1 — for when the royal root had seemed withered in dry ground, to behold a king of the house of David was a pleasing surprise, and they ran in transports of joy, praising the king and praising God, having with them such as taught to sing praise. Then Athaliah slain: she ran, Henry says, upon the very point of the sword of justice. Imagining her interest far better than it was, she ventured into the house of the LORD and cried "Treason, treason!" — but nobody seconded her, nobody sided with her; the pride of her heart had deceived her, for she thought all her own when none were cordially so.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch place the scene in its frame, the slaughter of Athaliah told here as in 2 Kings 11:13-16, and note that the Chronicler has expanded the older account of the people's instruments with his characteristic addition of the singers and those who led the praise. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the noise that drew the queen more precisely — the noise of the people, the couriers, and those who were acclaiming the king — comparing the slightly different wording of the parallel, where "the people" may be an inadvertent repetition of the scribe's pen.

What the witnesses together catch is the terrible aptness of Athaliah's end. She is drawn to her death by the very sound of joy; the acclamation of the rightful king is the summons that brings the murderess of the royal seed into the open. She had spent six years thinking the throne secured to her by the blood she had shed; and now, at the noise of a nation's gladness, she walks unguarded into the temple she had scorned and finds not a single friend. The arch-traitor cries "Treason" against the true heir — the last self-deception of a heart that had mistaken its own security to the end. Henry's phrase gathers it up: she ran upon the point of the sword of justice. The joy of the delivered people and the exposure of the tyrant are, in the Chronicler's telling, a single moment: the same cry that crowns the son of David unmasks the woman who had tried to blot his line from the earth.
13:
Athaliah's own eyes take in the scene that condemns her, and the witnesses attend to the royal tableau she beholds. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the details with care: the king was "standing" at his pillar — better, upon his stand or station, the appointed royal place answering to the "stand" of the parallel in 2 Kings 11:14 — at the entrance, with the princes and the trumpeters beside him. The people were "rejoicing and sounding," and here the Chronicler adds what Kings lacks: the minstrels with their instruments of music and the men who led the chanting, literally those who "taught to praise" — one of the writer's characteristic enlargements of the older text. Where Kings says the queen "cried," the Chronicler says she "said," a lesser word.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley catches the wonder in the people's joy with the same figure Henry used: they rejoiced to see a rod sprung out of the stem of Jesse, to see what they had despaired of ever seeing, a king of the house of David. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, reading this verse and the last as one, dwells on the contrast between that national gladness and the solitary fury of Athaliah, who rent her clothes and cried treason while not a soul stood with her. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply gather the run of verses under the head of Athaliah's slaughter, told as in the parallel.

The witnesses converge on the significance of the picture the queen is forced to see. The king stands where a king should stand, at his own pillar, hedged by princes and heralded by trumpets, and the whole apparatus of temple praise — singers, players, leaders of the chant — breaks over the scene like a wave. It is the very thing Athaliah had spent six years to make impossible, and it stands before her complete. Her rent garments are the ancient sign of grief and horror, and her cry of "treason" is the final irony of a reign founded on treason: the one true act of loyalty in the kingdom, the crowning of David's heir, she can name only as rebellion. The Chronicler's added detail of the Levitical music is not idle ornament; it marks that this is worship as much as coronation, the restored praise of the house of God rising at the same instant as the restored throne of David. Against that swelling chorus the childless, friendless queen stands alone, seeing with her own eyes the promise she could not kill — and the sight is her sentence.
14:
Sentence passes into execution, and the witnesses weigh both the order and the reverence that governs it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads Jehoiada's command against any who should side with the queen as a plain measure of security: whoever takes her part, or endeavours to prevent the present revolution, is to be slain at once — the rising must not be allowed to falter for want of resolution. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes the verse follows 2 Kings 11:15 closely, with a few formal variations; the Chronicler's "brought out" stands where Kings has "commanded," two Hebrew words so nearly alike that one may be a corruption of the other. The charge "have her forth of the ranges" he renders "make her go out between the ranks of the guards" — she is to be led out through the lane of soldiers — and Jehoiada's "slay her not in the house of the LORD" he takes as the emphatic "ye must not slay her."

That last clause is the heart of the verse for the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry. Jehoiada, as protector in the king's minority, ordered the queen to be slain; but special care was taken that she should not be slain within the house of the LORD, for, as Henry finely puts it, that sacred place must not be so far disgraced, nor that wicked woman so far honoured. To shed even a murderess's blood in the sanctuary would have profaned the one and dignified the other; better to lead her out to a common place and let justice be done beyond the holy ground.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the verse in its narrative course, part of the slaughter of Athaliah told as in the parallel account. What the witnesses share is a sense of the discipline that runs through even this violent hour. The order is decisive — any who rally to the queen die with her — yet the decisiveness is fenced by reverence: the execution is to be swift but not sacrilegious, carried out beyond the temple's threshold. The same jealousy for the holiness of the house that kept the armed people in the courts and reserved the sanctuary to the priests now keeps the queen's blood off the pavement of God's dwelling. Justice will have its due, and the usurper who slew the seed royal will not escape; but she will not be given the grim distinction of dying where the LORD had set his name. Jehoiada's men lay hold of her and hurry her out through the ranks, and the sentence waits for ground less holy than this.
15:
The place of Athaliah's death is fixed with a grim exactness, and the witnesses read the geography as the completion of Jehoiada's care. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects the opening clause: "they laid hands on her" is rather "they made way for her on both sides," the guards parting to open a lane through which the queen was hurried — the reading supported by the Greek and the Syriac, which have them "make room for her." She is not so much seized as swept out between the ranks. The "entering of the horse gate by the king's house" answers to the parallel in 2 Kings 11:16, which tells how she went by the way of the entry of the horses into the king's house; the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, glossing the same horse gate, simply refers the reader there.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the notice in its place as the close of the queen's slaughter, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks only that the sentence, once given, was done immediately. But the witnesses together let the location speak. Athaliah is led out of the temple, whose holiness was not to be stained with her blood, and back toward the palace she had usurped; and it is there, at the horse gate by the king's house, that she is slain. The woman who had reached the throne over the corpses of the royal seed dies at the threshold of the very house she had seized, on common ground fit for the death of a usurper, among the horses and the traffic of the palace rather than in the courts of God.

There is a measured justice in it that the witnesses feel without labouring. She had profaned the throne of David; she dies at the door of the palace. She had scorned the house of the LORD; she is denied even the dark honour of dying within it. The guards who made way for her on either side open, in effect, the road to her execution, and the queen passes down it to the place appointed. The Chronicler's brief sentence thus rounds off the reverent scruple of the preceding verse: the sanctuary is kept undefiled, and yet the sentence is not softened. Justice is neither hurried into the holy place nor set aside for its sake, but carried out fully at the horse gate, where the usurpation had had its seat. So the six years of tyranny end where they had reigned, at the king's house, and the last obstacle to the son of David is removed from the earth.
16:
With the usurper dead, the witnesses turn to the covenant that refounds the kingdom, and they fasten together on the little word "him." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks a slight but characteristic variation from 2 Kings 11:17, which speaks of "the covenant between Jehovah and the king and the people." The Chronicler writes rather "between him, and all the people, and the king," and Ellicott takes that "him" to be the high priest himself, regarded as representing Jehovah in the transaction — a phrasing that avoids the apparent irreverence of making the Deity a direct co-partner with men in a compact. The aim, he adds, is literally that they should "become a people for Jehovah"; and he notes that Kings preserves a further clause, "between the king and the people," relating to those limitations of the royal prerogative that were usually agreed upon at a reign's beginning, as when Israel covenanted with David in 2 Samuel 5:3 and Samuel wrote the manner of the kingdom in 1 Samuel 10:25.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the "him" the same way: the high priest was on this occasion the representative of God, whom both the people and the king must have had in view through the medium of his priest. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds the whole as a threefold indenture, tripartite yet with one true intent — that they should be the LORD's people. God covenanted, by Jehoiada, to take them for his people; the king and people covenanted to be his; and then the king covenanted to govern them as the people of God, and the people to be subject to the king in the fear of God and for his sake. Jehoiada, Henry says, acted here as God's priest and representative, a sort of mediator, as Moses had been.

A quieter dissent belongs to the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley, who glosses the "him" not as the priest but directly as the LORD, understanding the covenant, as the parallel expressly puts it, to be between Jehovah and the king and people. So the witnesses circle a small but real question — whether the first party to the compact is God himself, named by the pronoun, or the high priest standing in God's stead — without letting it divide them on the substance. All agree that the covenant binds the nation Godward, that Jehoiada mediates it, and that its whole burden is the recovery of a people for the LORD. Henry turns it into a charge for every reader: to look upon ourselves and one another as the LORD's people is the spring of all our duty, to God and to man alike. The throne is restored in the verses before; here the deeper thing is restored, the bond that makes Israel God's.
17:
The reformation goes beyond the throne to the altar, and the witnesses read the fall of Baal's house as the truer heart of the day's work. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry states the principle outright: they would not have done half their work had they destroyed only the usurper of the king's right and not the usurper of God's right, asserting the honour of the throne but not that of the altar. The great grievance of Athaliah's reign had been the bringing in of the worship of Baal, and so that must be abolished first of all — down with Baal's house, his altars, his images, and let the blood of his priest be mingled with his sacrifices, for God had commanded in Deut. 13:5-6 that seducers to idolatry should be put to death. The slaying of Mattan the priest of Baal before his own altars is, on Henry's reading, not savagery but obedience to the law of the LORD.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds a telling philological touch: the Targum will not so much as dignify Mattan with the title "priest," but calls him a cumera, a priestling — the paraphrast refusing to lend the honourable word to a servant of the idol. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the verbs of demolition — they "pulled down" the house and "broke in pieces" its altars — and notes that the parallel in 2 Kings 11:18 adds that they broke them "thoroughly," the work left half-done nowhere. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply carry the account forward, this destruction of Baal-worship standing, with the covenant before it and the temple's restoration after, as the middle term of the whole reformation.

The witnesses do not divide; together they insist that the coup was a religious act before it was a political one. Athaliah's death removed a usurper; the razing of Baal's temple removed the usurpation of God's own honour, which was the deeper treason. Henry's balance holds the two together — throne and altar, the king's right and God's right — and makes the second the weightier: a revolution that had merely changed the occupant of the palace while leaving the idol standing would have been no true restoration at all. It is fitting, then, that Mattan falls before his altars as Athaliah fell at the palace gate, each struck down at the seat of the false power he served. The people who had covenanted in the verse before to be the LORD's now prove the covenant in deed, turning at once from the oath to the demolition, so that the first-fruit of being God's people is the pulling down of the god that was not God.
18:
With Baal thrown down, the witnesses watch the true worship restored to its channels, and they mark the double authority behind the ordering. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that this verse and the next are a thoroughly characteristic expansion of the brief notice in Kings that "the priest set officers over the house of the LORD." He renders the Chronicler's fuller phrase, "Jehoiada put the offices of the house of the LORD into the hand of the priests the Levites," those whom David had distributed into their courses, as recorded in 1 Chron. 23:6. The burnt offerings are to be made "as it is written in the law of Moses," a plain reference to the Pentateuch, and the service performed "with rejoicing and with singing, as it was ordained by David." The meaning of the whole, Ellicott sums up, is that the high priest now restored the regular temple services as David had arranged them, which had been neglected, or at best irregularly kept, through the six years of Athaliah's usurpation.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley makes the same point on the idiom: "appointed" is in the Hebrew "put the offices of the house of the LORD into the hand," that is, Jehoiada restored the priests and Levites to the exercise of their office. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the notice along with the surrounding acts of restoration, one piece of Jehoiada's larger work of setting the kingdom in order.

It is the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry who draws out the theology of the arrangement. The temple service had been neglected in the late reigns, the priests and people wanting either power or zeal to keep it up under princes disaffected to it; now Jehoiada restored the offices to their proper courses and proper hands — the priests to their courses for the due offering of sacrifice according to the law of Moses, and the singers to theirs according to the appointment of David. Henry notes the two authorities working in concert: Moses for the sacrifice, David for the song, the Pentateuch and the psalmody together. And he catches the note of gladness the verse strikes, for the sacrifices were offered with rejoicing and singing, and with good reason — "we joy in God," he says, citing Rom. 5:11, "when we receive the atonement." The witnesses converge: the pulling down of Baal is completed only in the setting up of true worship, and the restored king's first care, through his priestly guardian, is that the house of God should sing and sacrifice again by the old and lawful orders. Reformation is not merely the destruction of the false but the reinstatement of the true, and its proper sound is joy.
19:
The restoration reaches even to the gates, and the witnesses read the stationing of the porters as the guarding of the temple's holiness. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that Jehoiada "stationed," or appointed, the porters at — or rather over — the gates of the house of the LORD, the doorkeepers whose posts David had assigned in 1 Chron. 26:1 and following. Their charge was that none who was unclean in any thing should enter in — a rule Ellicott ties both to the earlier direction of v.6, that the people not presume into the holy place, and to the Mosaic laws of purity that shut out the defiled, such as the exclusion from the camp commanded in Num. 5:2.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the notice in the run of restorations, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies its sense: the porters were put in their respective posts as David had ordered, and their office was to take care that none who were upon any account ceremonially unclean should be admitted into the courts of the temple. The gatekeepers are not menial guards but ministers of holiness, set to keep the boundary of the sacred that this same chapter has insisted on from the first.

The witnesses converge on the completeness of the reform. It was not enough to restore the sacrifices and the singers; the very thresholds must be watched, so that the purity of the house should be maintained day by day and not only in the hour of its rededication. The zeal that fenced the sanctuary during the coup, keeping the armed people in the courts, is now made a standing institution: doorkeepers at every gate, charged to turn back the unclean. There is a fitting order in the Chronicler's account — Baal's house pulled down, the LORD's service set up, and now the LORD's house hedged about against defilement — so that the reformation moves from the destruction of the false, through the reinstatement of the true, to the daily safeguarding of the holy. Henry's stress on David's arrangement binds the whole together: what Jehoiada restores is not a novelty but the ancient pattern, the courses of priests and singers and porters alike as the man after God's own heart had ordained them. The kingdom is refounded not by invention but by return, and even its gates are set to remember that the house belongs to a holy God, whose courts the unclean may not tread.
20:
The last act brings the king from the temple to the throne, and the witnesses follow the solemn procession that perfects the revolution. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the company that escorts him — the captains of hundreds, the nobles, the governors of the people, and all the people of the land. Where Kings had named the guard by their obscure foreign titles, the Carians and the couriers, the Chronicler writes "nobles" and "governors of the people"; these, Ellicott suggests, are perhaps the heads of the clans gathered in v.2 and the princes of v.13, though the substitution looks partly like an attempt to explain the old guard-titles the writer no longer understood. They "brought down the king from the house of the LORD," and came through the high gate into the king's house — the gate Kings calls the couriers' gate, which may have borne the name "high" as the grand entrance to the palace, a designation a temple gate also carries in 2 Chron. 27:3.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the verse in the sequence of the restoration, the enthronement following the covenant and the cleansing as the parallel account has it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the movement its meaning: the civil government was now re-established, for they brought the king in state to his own palace and set him upon the throne of the kingdom, to give law and give judgment, whether in his own person or, while he was yet a child, by Jehoiada his guardian. Thus, Henry says, was this happy revolution perfected.

The witnesses feel the fitness of the two houses in the verse. The boy is crowned in the house of the LORD, where the promise to David was kept and the covenant renewed; and from there he is led down and through the high gate to the house of the king, to take the seat of rule. The order is not accidental: the throne is entered by way of the temple, the king's authority received in the sanctuary before it is exercised in the palace. Ellicott's careful sorting of the escort — nobles, governors, captains, and the whole people of the land — marks how broad the consent to the new reign was, the same national breadth seen when the Levites and family chiefs were first summoned. And Henry's note that the child would rule for a time through his priestly guardian looks quietly ahead, for the reign of Joash will prove good only so long as Jehoiada stands beside the throne. For now the revolution is complete: the son of David crowned, the covenant sworn, Baal thrown down, the temple restored, and the king set upon his throne with the people rejoicing about him.
21:
The chapter closes on peace, and the witnesses read the quiet of the city as the seal of a work well done. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes the plain sense first: the city was quiet because there was no attempt at a counter-revolution — the change was so complete and so welcome that no party rose to reverse it. He then passes on a curious tradition from the Targum touching the crown set on Joash in v.11. According to the paraphrast, this was the royal crown David had taken from the head of the king of the Ammonites, set with a precious loadstone in which was engraven the great and honourable Name of the LORD, and weighing a talent of gold; it was a standing testimony to the house of David that no king who was not of David's seed could bear it upon his head or endure its weight, so that when the people saw it rest upon Joash and saw him bear it, they believed him to be of the seed of David and made him king. Clarke reports the legend as the Jews' own, resting on Rashi, without adopting it — a fanciful witness to the conviction that the throne belonged to David's line alone.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the verse as Henry does: the generality of the people rejoiced, while the rest were quiet and made no opposition. And both the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and Wesley lift the closing scene into a figure of the soul, for, as they put it in almost the same words, when the Son of David is enthroned in the soul all therein is quiet, and springs of joy are opened. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch let the notice stand as the settled end of the whole account, the rest that follows the removal of Athaliah.

The witnesses gather on the chapter's final mood. The death of the usurper, far from plunging the land into strife, brings it rest; the joy that broke out at the coronation settles into a lasting quiet, the peace of a kingdom returned to its rightful king and its rightful God. Clarke's Targumic tale, whatever its worth as history, catches the truth the whole chapter has pressed — that Joash reigns because he is David's seed, the heir of an unbreakable promise. Henry and Wesley make the last application the abiding one: what happened in Jerusalem when the son of David was crowned and Baal cast down is what happens in a heart when the greater Son of David is enthroned there — the usurper deposed, the true King owned, and all within made quiet and glad. So the chapter that opened in the darkness of Athaliah's tyranny ends in light, in joy, and in rest.
